title: Teamwork and Leadership Skills
summary: Learn how to set shared goals, run meetings, share work fairly, give feedback, handle conflict and lead others, in school projects and at work.

body.p: A team is more than a group of people sitting together. A group becomes a team when everyone understands the same goal and knows what part they play in reaching it. Many student projects fail not because members are lazy or weak, but because nobody ever said clearly what the project was for or who would do what.

list: Coordinator: keeps track of the plan and reminds people of deadlines. This is not a boss; it is a helper for the whole team.
Ideas person: suggests approaches and asks 'what if we tried this?'
Checker: reads work for mistakes, missing parts and whether it answers the task.
Note-taker: records decisions and who agreed to do what.
Presenter or spokesperson: shares the final result with the teacher, class or client.
Researcher: finds facts, sources and examples.

body.p: One person can hold more than one role, and roles can rotate between tasks. The point is that each important job has a name next to it. If 'checking the work' belongs to everybody, it usually belongs to nobody.

A good team goal is specific, has a deadline and can be checked. 'Do well in the science project' is weak. 'Hand in a 10-slide presentation on water pollution by Friday 12:00, with every claim backed by one source' is strong, because the team can look at it on Friday and say yes or no.

steps: Read the task or brief together and underline what the teacher or client has asked for.
Agree in one sentence what a successful result looks like.
Write down the deadline and any smaller deadlines on the way.
List the jobs that must be done and match each to a role.
Ask each member what they can offer and what worries them.
Write the goal and roles where everyone can see them, for example in a shared chat pinned message.

body.p: Worked example: four classmates, Kofi, Zainab, Ngozi and Tendai, must make a poster on recycling for a school fair. They agree the goal: 'One A1 poster, readable from two metres, with three facts and one local example, ready by Thursday.' Kofi coordinates, Zainab researches, Ngozi designs, Tendai checks spelling and facts. When Zainab falls ill, the team knows exactly which job is uncovered and Tendai takes over research for a day.

body.tip: Write the team goal in one sentence before anyone starts work. If the team cannot agree on one sentence, you have found a problem early, which is cheaper than finding it the night before the deadline.

lessons.title: Running a meeting: agenda, notes, actions

body.p: Most team meetings are wasted because nobody knows why they are happening. A short, well-run meeting of 20 minutes can replace days of confused messages. A meeting can be in a classroom, under a tree, or on a phone call. The same simple structure works everywhere.

list: Decide the purpose in one line, for example 'Choose our topic and divide the research'.
Write an agenda of two to four items, each with a time limit.
Tell people the time, place or link and how long it will last.
Ask members to bring anything needed, such as their draft or a list of ideas.

body.p: Choose a chair to keep time and make sure everyone can speak, and a note-taker to write down decisions. The chair's job is not to talk the most. If one person dominates, the chair can say, 'Thanks, Chidi. Let us hear from Amara and Joseph before we decide.' If the talk drifts off the topic, note the new idea in a 'parking list' to discuss later.

body.code:
Meeting: Science project planning
Date: Tuesday, 4:00-4:20 pm
Present: Amara, Chidi, Joseph, Esi

Agenda
1. Choose topic (5 min)
2. Share out research (10 min)
3. Next steps (5 min)

Decisions
- Topic: rainwater harvesting

Actions
- Amara: find 2 sources by Friday
- Chidi: draft intro by Sunday
- Joseph: collect photos by Saturday
- Esi: check draft and send feedback Monday

body.p: Send the notes to everyone within 24 hours, even if your group is only on a messaging app. An action is only real when it has a name, a task and a date. 'Someone will look for sources' is not an action; 'Amara will find two sources by Friday' is. At the start of the next meeting, begin by reviewing the actions: done, not done, or needs help.

body.tip: End every meeting by having the note-taker read the actions aloud. This takes 30 seconds and catches most misunderstandings before they cost you a week.

lessons.title: Sharing work fairly in group projects

body.p: Unfair workload is the most common complaint in group projects. Usually one or two people end up doing most of the work, while others feel they were not given a chance, or did not know what to do. Fair does not always mean identical. It means the load matches the time and skills each person has, and everyone can see that it does.

body.h: Step one: break the project into tasks

body.p: You cannot share a lump called 'the project'. Break it into tasks small enough that each can be finished and checked. For a research report these might be: research background, collect data, write the introduction, write the findings, make charts, check references, edit the whole report and prepare the presentation.

Give each task a rough number of hours. Suppose the team estimates 30 hours of total work for four people. An equal share is 30 divided by 4, which is 7.5 hours each. Now compare that with real life. If Tendai has football training and a part-time job and can offer only 4 hours, the others must cover the difference: 26 hours across three people is about 8.7 hours each. Being open about this early prevents resentment later.

steps: List all the tasks and estimate hours for each.
Ask each member how many hours they can honestly give each week.
Match tasks to strengths where possible, but make sure everyone also does some necessary but boring work.
Write who does what, with a deadline, in the meeting notes.
Check progress halfway, not on the last day.
If someone falls behind, ask what help they need before assuming laziness.

body.p: Esi is good at design and offers to do all the slides. That seems helpful, but it leaves her with the longest task while others do small jobs. The team instead gives Esi the slide design, and the other three each write the content for one section that Esi will format. The workload becomes more balanced and Esi's skill is still used.

body.tip: Make contributions visible. A shared document with names beside tasks, or a simple tick list, lets everyone see progress and makes quiet free-riding much harder.

lessons.title: Giving and receiving feedback, and handling conflict

body.p: Feedback is information that helps someone improve. Conflict is a disagreement that, if handled badly, damages the team. Both skills use the same core habit: talk about the work and the behaviour, not about the person's character.

Useful feedback is specific, kind and focused on what can change. Compare 'Your section is bad' with 'Your section has good facts, but the second paragraph does not explain how the facts connect. Could you add one sentence that links them?' The second version names one strength, one problem and one next step.

list: Start with something specific that works.
Describe one or two issues you can point to in the work.
Suggest a next step or ask a question.
Choose a time when the person can listen, not just before they present.

body.p: When you receive feedback, your first reaction may be to defend yourself. Try instead to listen to the end, ask a question to understand, and say thank you. You do not have to agree with every point, but think about it before you decide. If you are upset, you can say, 'Thanks, let me think about that and come back to you tomorrow.'
Scenario: Joseph keeps arriving late to meetings, and Amara is annoyed and starts criticising him in the group chat. This usually makes things worse. A better path is a private, calm conversation.

steps: Pick a private moment and say you want to solve a problem together.
Describe what happened without blame: 'In the last three meetings we started 15 minutes late.'
Say the effect: 'We then had to rush the decisions.'
Ask for his view: 'What is making it hard to arrive on time?'
Listen. Joseph may have a bus that is always late.
Agree on a solution together, such as moving the meeting later, and check back in a week.

body.p: If you cannot solve it between yourselves, ask a neutral person such as a teacher, lecturer or supervisor to help. That is not a failure; it is a sensible use of support.

body.tip: Use 'I' statements: 'I felt stressed when the work arrived late' lands better than 'You are always late', because it describes your experience rather than attacking.

body.p: In a school, a university or an online course, you will work with people who differ from you in language, culture, religion, age, ability, confidence and background. These differences can make a team stronger because members bring different knowledge. They can also cause misunderstanding if we assume everyone communicates the way we do.

list: Language: someone may be fluent in their first language but still learning yours. Fast speech, slang and jokes are easily missed.
Directness: in some settings, saying 'no' directly is normal; in others it is considered rude, and people say 'we will see' instead.
Time: for some, a 4 pm meeting means exactly 4 pm; for others it means roughly then.
Confidence: some people speak up quickly; others think before talking, or were taught not to question older people.
Access: a teammate may have a weak data connection or share a phone with family.

body.p: Use plain words and short sentences. Check understanding by asking people to say back what they heard: 'Can you tell me in your own words what you will do?' Give quiet members a way in, such as asking each person for one idea in turn, or letting people add ideas in writing. Do not assume silence means agreement or lack of ideas.

Worked example: Grace, who studies in Accra, works in an online team with Lucia in Madrid and Daniel in Nairobi. Their first call is hard because the connection drops, and Lucia speaks quickly. They agree to use a shared document for key decisions, short voice notes instead of video when data is limited, and a meeting time that is sensible for all three time zones. After that, work moves much more smoothly.

body.tip: When you are unsure what someone meant, ask a friendly question instead of guessing. 'Do you mean we should start now or wait until Friday?' takes five seconds and avoids days of confusion.

lessons.title: Leading without a title, delegating and motivating

body.p: Leadership is not only for the head boy, the captain or the manager. You lead whenever you help a group move in a useful direction. In a group project with no chosen leader, the person who suggests a plan, welcomes quieter members and follows up on actions is leading, even without a title.

body.h: What leading without a title looks like

list: Offer a first step when the group is stuck: 'Shall we list the tasks first?'
Say thank you when someone does good work.
Keep the group on the goal when the talk drifts.
Admit your own mistakes quickly.
Do your own part well. People follow people who deliver.

body.p: Delegating means giving someone responsibility for a task. Many new leaders do it badly by saying 'Can you do the research?' without any detail. A good handover covers what the result should look like, the deadline, what help is available, and how you will check in.

body.code:
Weak:   'Please do the research.'

Strong: 'Please find three reliable sources on rainwater harvesting
        and write two sentences about each. I need them by
        Friday 5 pm. Message me if you get stuck by Wednesday.'

body.p: People work harder when they understand why the job matters, feel trusted, and see their effort noticed. Instead of 'Just finish your part', try 'Your charts are what will make the findings clear to the examiners, so I really need them to be good.' Match the task to the person where you can, and offer support rather than pressure when someone struggles.

Scenario: Tendai has not started his section and the deadline is two days away. A weak response is to take over silently and resent him. A stronger one is to ask privately, 'How is your section going? Is there anything I can help with?' You may learn that he did not understand the task, and a ten-minute explanation solves the problem.

body.tip: Delegate the whole task, not tiny pieces, and then resist checking every hour. Agree one check-in point, and trust the person until then.

body.p: Finishing a project is not the end of the learning. Reflection means looking back at what happened, understanding why, and deciding what you will do differently next time. Teams that skip this repeat the same mistakes in every project. Employers and universities often ask for examples of teamwork, and honest reflection gives you real examples.

steps: What was the goal and did we achieve it?
What went well, and what did I do that helped?
What did not go well, and what part did I play in that?
What did I learn about working with others?
What one thing will I do differently next time?

body.p: After a group history presentation, Chidi writes: 'Our goal was a 10-minute presentation with sources. We finished on time and the teacher said our timeline was clear. I helped by making the task list at the first meeting. What went badly was that we only practised once, and I rushed my part because I was nervous. I also did not ask Esi for feedback until the day before. Next time I will book a practice session two days before the deadline and ask for feedback earlier.'
Notice that Chidi gives facts, names his own part and ends with a specific action. He does not blame others or make vague promises such as 'be better'.

list: Hold a 15-minute review meeting after the deadline.
Each person shares one thing that worked and one thing to change.
Keep the tone about processes, not people.
Write down two or three agreed lessons and save them for the next project.

body.p: You can also use reflection to describe your skills in a CV or interview. A statement such as 'I organised weekly meetings for a group of four and tracked actions in a shared list, which helped us submit on time' is much stronger than 'I am a good team player'.

body.tip: Write your reflection within a few days of finishing. Details fade quickly, and a short note while it is fresh is worth more than a long one written a month later.

quiz.q: Your group of four has a project due Friday. Nobody has said who will do what, and each person assumes someone else is organising. What is the best first move?
options: Wait until Wednesday to see whether someone else takes charge, then help with whatever is left
Start writing the whole project yourself so it is not late, and tell the others only when it is done
Send a message to the group saying it is badly organised and that someone else should fix it
Suggest a short meeting to agree the goal, list the tasks and put a name and deadline beside each

quiz.q: Which of these is the strongest team goal?
options: Do a really good job on the science project and make sure that everyone in the team enjoys it
Try our best and work together as a team so that the final result is something we are proud of
Hand in a 10-slide presentation on water pollution by Friday 12:00, with every claim sourced
Make the presentation much better than last time, with more effort and more interesting content

quiz.q: At the end of a meeting, the note-taker records: 'Someone will find sources.' What is wrong with this action?
options: It is too short to be useful, as a good action needs at least two sentences
It should have been written before the meeting, so that members could prepare for it
Actions should be about decisions and not about tasks, so it belongs in another section
It has no named person and no deadline, so nobody is clearly responsible for doing it

quiz.q: In a meeting one member keeps talking and two others have said nothing. As chair, what do you do?
options: Let the discussion carry on because the loudest person probably has the best idea
Thank the speaker and invite the quieter members to share their ideas before deciding
End the meeting and decide the plan by yourself afterwards, because you are the chair
Tell the talkative member to stop attending future meetings so the others can speak

quiz.q: A team estimates 30 hours of work. Four members share it equally, but one can give only 4 hours. Which is the most reasonable approach?
options: Give everyone 7.5 hours anyway, even though one cannot do that much, and accept a late project
Be open about it and share the remaining 26 hours among the other three, about 8.7 hours each
Remove the member from the team without discussing it, then split 30 hours among three
Let the member do nothing, say nothing to the teacher, and hope the other three cope

quiz.q: Esi is the best designer and offers to make all the slides. What should the team consider?
options: Accept at once, because she volunteered and is the best designer, so the matter is closed
Refuse her offer, because team members should avoid using their strengths on the project
Ask her to do all the slides and also all the research, since she is clearly the most capable person
Her skill is useful, but giving her all the slides may overload her, so share the writing among others

quiz.q: A teammate hands in a section with good facts but a confusing order. Which feedback is most useful?
options: Your facts are strong. The order of paragraphs two and three is confusing; could you try swapping them?
This section is poor and very confusing, so please fix it properly before anyone else has to read it
You are not good at writing, so maybe someone else in the group should write this part
Nothing needs to change, it looks fine to me, so let us move on to the next section

quiz.q: Someone criticises your work in a way that stings. What is the most constructive response?
options: Point out the faults in their own work straight away, so that the criticism feels fair to both
Listen to the end, ask a clarifying question, thank them, and decide afterwards what to change
Say nothing, stop speaking to them for the rest of the project, and avoid their feedback
Agree with everything they say straight away to end the conversation, and change all of it

quiz.q: Joseph is often 15 minutes late. Amara is annoyed. What should she do first?
options: Talk with Joseph privately, describe what happened and ask what makes it hard to arrive on time
Post in the group chat that Joseph is unreliable and ask everyone to remind him of the time
Say nothing to Joseph and secretly do his tasks yourself so that the work stays on schedule
Tell the teacher straight away that Joseph must be removed from the group for being late so often

quiz.q: Which statement is an 'I' statement suited to raising a problem?
options: I felt worried on Thursday when the draft had not arrived, because we had little time to check it
You finish everything late, and it makes the whole group look bad in front of the teacher
Everyone in the group knows you do not care about this project, because your draft was late
Typical of you to be late again with your draft, and now the rest of us must rescue the project

quiz.q: You work with a teammate who is still learning your language and often stays quiet in calls. Which habit helps most?
options: Speak faster so that the meeting is shorter, and move on once a few people have replied
Use plain words, check understanding by asking them to say it back, and invite written ideas too
Assume that silence means they agree with the group, and move on to the next point on the agenda
Leave them out of the discussions to avoid confusion, and send them the final decisions later

quiz.q: There is no appointed leader in your group. Which action best shows leading without a title?
options: Propose listing the tasks, invite each person's views and follow up on the agreed actions
Announce that you are now in charge and everyone must obey your instructions from today
Wait to be appointed by the teacher before doing anything that helps the group move on
Complain to other friends that nobody is leading, and hope that someone eventually steps up
Please do the research for our project and send me whatever you find as soon as you have some free time to spare.
Do the research somehow, I do not mind how you do it or when, as long as it is eventually finished.
I will do all of the research myself later in the week, so you can relax and just add your own parts at the end.
Please find three reliable sources and write two sentences on each by Friday 5 pm; message me by Wednesday if stuck.

quiz.q: Tendai has not started his section and the deadline is in two days. What is the most useful first step?
options: Quietly take over his section yourself and resent him, without telling anyone you did it
Tell the whole team in the group chat that he is lazy and has not started his work
Ask him privately how it is going and whether he needs help, since he may have misunderstood the task
Cut his name from the final submission without talking to him first, since he did not contribute anything

quiz.q: After a project, which reflection sentence is the most useful for future teamwork?
options: The project went okay in the end, and next time I will simply try to be better and to work a lot harder
Our group was bad because the others did not help me enough, and next time I want a completely different team
We practised only once and I rushed my part, so next time I will book a rehearsal two days before the deadline
Everything went perfectly, so there is nothing to change and next time we will do exactly the same things again
